title: Indian Society: Social Institutions: Continuity and Change

topics.title: Caste: varna, jati and its features

learn.hook: Caste, tribe and family are institutions you were born into without being asked. This chapter shows how each has stayed the same in some ways and changed in others. We begin with caste, a word that is not even Indian in origin.
points: Caste, tribe and family are key institutions of Indian society; each shows both continuity and change.
The English word 'caste' comes from the Portuguese 'casta' (pure breed). It is used for two Indian terms: varna and jati.
Varna (literally 'colour') is the fourfold all-India classification: Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya and Shudra, with a large group outside it, the 'outcastes' or untouchables (ati-shudra).
Jati is a generic term for species or kinds; jatis are local, regionally variable groups and are the real working units of caste. There are thousands of them.

Features: membership by birth; endogamy (marriage within the group); rules about food and sharing food; a hierarchy of rank; segmental sub-divisions (sub-castes); traditional link with hereditary occupations. Caste was less rigid in the early Vedic period and became rigid later.

example.q: A woman cannot change her jati by moving to another town, earning more or marrying outside. Which features of caste does this show?
steps: She was assigned her caste at birth: membership by birth.
Marriage is expected within the group: endogamy.
Earnings do not change caste rank: caste is ascribed, not achieved.
example.answer: Ascription by birth and endogamy, the two core features.

learn.reallife: Matrimonial columns that still specify caste show how endogamy, one of caste's oldest features, continues even in tech-savvy apps and newspapers.

Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra

The varnas are Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya and Shudra

Answer: Jatis are local groups that vary by region

quiz.q: Endogamy means:
options: Marrying outside one's own caste group
Having more than one spouse
Living with the husband's family
Marrying within one's own caste group

steps: Asks: the meaning of endogamy
Endogamy = marriage within one's own group
So marrying within one's own caste
Marrying outside the group is exogamy
Answer: Marrying within one's own caste group

quiz.q: 'Segmental organisation' of caste refers to:
options: Ranking of castes by wealth only
Separation of castes by region
Equal status of all castes
Division of castes into sub-castes
quiz.explain: Castes are divided into sub-castes and sometimes further.
steps: Asks: what segmental organisation means
Castes are divided into sub-castes, and sometimes further into smaller units
Ranking belongs to hierarchy, not segmentation
Answer: Division of castes into sub-castes

quiz.q: Which is NOT a traditional feature of caste?
options: Link with hereditary occupation
A hierarchy of ranked groups
Rules about sharing of food
Membership chosen by the individual
quiz.explain: Caste membership is fixed at birth.
steps: Asks: which is NOT a traditional feature of caste
Caste membership is fixed by birth
Hereditary occupation, hierarchy and food rules are all features
So 'membership chosen by the individual' is not
Answer: Membership chosen by the individual

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Caste is an ascribed status.
Reason (R): One is born into one's caste and cannot normally change it.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.explain: Ascribed status is given at birth, which is exactly how caste works.
steps: Check A: caste is an ascribed status: true
Check R: one is born into caste and cannot normally change it: true
R explains A: ascribed status is status given at birth
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R explains A

quiz.q: Historically, caste distinctions were:
options: Less rigid in the early Vedic period than later
Most rigid in the early Vedic period
Unchanged since the very earliest times
Created for the first time under colonial rule
quiz.explain: Caste rigidity increased in the post-Vedic period.
steps: Asks: how caste rigidity changed over history
Caste distinctions were less rigid in the early Vedic period
Rigidity increased in the post-Vedic period
"Created for the first time under colonial rule" is wrong because caste existed long before colonial rule
Answer: Less rigid in the early Vedic period than later

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Is caste the same as varna? And what makes caste different from just being in a club?'
teach.praise: So varna is the fourfold scheme, jati is the real local group, and you're born into it and marry within it. Not a club at all!
teach.nudge: But how are varna and jati different, and what are caste's main features?

revise.summary: 'Caste' is used for two Indian terms: varna, the fourfold all-India classification, and jati, the local, regionally variable groups that are the real working units. Caste membership is by birth and marked by endogamy, food rules, hierarchy and sub-divisions.
focus: Difference between varna and jati
The features of caste: birth, endogamy, food rules, hierarchy, segmental sub-divisions, hereditary occupations
Caste as an ascribed status
remember: 'Caste' comes from the Portuguese 'casta' (pure breed)
Varna: Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra, with the 'outcastes' or untouchables (ati-shudra) outside it
Endogamy: marriage within one's own caste group
Segmental organisation: division of castes into sub-castes
traps: Don't confuse endogamy with exogamy
Don't confuse jati with varna; jatis are local and number in thousands
Caste was not always rigid; it was less rigid in the early Vedic period

topics.title: Separation and hierarchy: caste's two principles

learn.hook: Caste works like two rules running at once: keep groups apart, and arrange them in a ladder. Together they create a system that is both divided and whole.
points: Principle 1, difference and separation: each caste is supposed to be different from and separate from others, through rules on marriage, food, social interaction and occupation.
Principle 2, wholeness and hierarchy: the separated castes are not equal; they fit into a hierarchical whole, like parts of a body, each with its place.
The hierarchy is based on the distinction between 'purity' and 'pollution': castes considered ritually pure are ranked higher, those considered impure lower.
In theory ritual status and material (economic, political) status could be separate. In practice they usually coincided: upper castes tended to hold land and power, lower castes tended to be poor.

example.q: Explain how rules about who may cook for whom express both principles of caste.
steps: Separation: castes keep apart by not sharing cooked food freely.
Hierarchy: food usually flows from higher to lower, not the reverse, because of purity rules.
So one practice both divides groups and ranks them.
example.answer: Food rules separate castes and rank them by purity and pollution.

learn.reallife: Practices like separate utensils for some guests, still reported in surveys in parts of India, show how ideas of purity and pollution can linger in daily life.

steps: Asks: the two organising principles of caste

options: Purity and pollution

quiz.explain: Ritual purity ranks castes higher, pollution lower.
steps: Asks: the basis of caste hierarchy

Answer: Purity and pollution

quiz.q: Which practice best expresses the principle of separation?
options: Ranking all castes in order from top to bottom
Equal access for all castes to village wells
Free choice of occupation for every person
Strict rules against marrying outside the caste
quiz.explain: Endogamy keeps castes separate.

Separation keeps castes apart, for example by endogamy
Strict rules against marrying outside the caste do this
Ranking castes illustrates hierarchy instead
Answer: Strict rules against marrying outside the caste

quiz.q: The 'wholeness' principle of caste suggests that:
options: All castes are equal parts of one common system
Castes have no relation of any kind with one another
Each caste forms a separate small state of its own
Separate castes fit together as ranked parts of one system
quiz.explain: Like parts of a body, castes have unequal places in the whole.

Separate castes fit together like parts of one body
But the parts have unequal, ranked places in the whole

Answer: Separate castes fit together as ranked parts of one system

quiz.q: In practice, how were ritual status and economic status related?
options: They usually coincided
They were always opposite
Ritual status had no meaning
Lower castes held most land
quiz.explain: Upper castes generally also held land and power.
steps: Asks: how ritual and economic status were related in practice
Upper castes generally also held land and power
So ritual and economic status usually coincided
"Lower castes held most land" is the reverse of the actual pattern
Answer: They usually coincided
quiz.mistake: Believes ritual and material status were separate in practice

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Caste is a system of both difference and inequality.
Reason (R): Castes are separated by rules and ranked by purity and pollution.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: The two principles together make caste both divided and unequal.
steps: Check A: caste is a system of difference and inequality: true
Check R: castes are separated by rules and ranked by purity and pollution: true
R explains A: separation gives difference, ranking gives inequality
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Sees only one of the two principles

quiz.q: Rules that cooked food may be accepted from some castes but not others are an example of:
options: Neither separation nor hierarchy
Only economic exchange
Both separation and hierarchy
Only regional custom
quiz.explain: Food rules divide groups and rank them by purity.
steps: Asks: what food-acceptance rules illustrate
The rules divide groups (separation)
They also rank groups by purity, since food is accepted only from some (hierarchy)
So both separation and hierarchy
Answer: Both separation and hierarchy
quiz.mistake: Sees food rules as merely custom

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Upper castes were generally the economically powerful groups in traditional society.
Reason (R): Caste rank and material status tended to coincide.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: The coincidence of ritual and material status explains upper-caste economic power.
steps: Check A: upper castes were generally economically powerful: true
Check R: caste rank and material status tended to coincide: true
R explains A: high ritual rank usually came with land and power
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Misses the overlap of caste and class

teach.ask: Gappu twitters: 'If castes are kept separate, how can they also be part of one system?'
teach.praise: Separate but stacked! Castes are kept apart and also ranked in one whole by purity and pollution.
teach.nudge: But what are the two principles, and what is the hierarchy based on?

revise.summary: Caste works on two principles: difference and separation, and wholeness and hierarchy. The hierarchy rests on purity and pollution, and in practice ritual status and economic status usually coincided.
focus: The two organising principles: separation and hierarchy
Purity and pollution as the basis of the hierarchy
How food rules show both principles at once
The overlap of ritual and material status
remember: Principle 1: difference and separation; Principle 2: wholeness and hierarchy
Caste hierarchy is based on the distinction between 'purity' and 'pollution'
traps: 'Wholeness' does not mean equal; castes fit together as ranked parts
Don't think hierarchy was based only on wealth
Ritual and material status were not separate in practice; they usually coincided

learn.hook: When British officials tried to count and rank every caste in the 1901 census, thousands of petitions arrived demanding a higher place. Counting caste changed caste.
points: Colonial rulers tried to understand Indian society in order to govern it. Systematic enumeration of caste began with the census.

The 1901 census, under Herbert Risley, tried to collect information on the social hierarchy of castes, i.e. their order of social precedence in each region. This made caste identities more rigid and sparked petitions from castes claiming higher status.
Colonial land revenue settlements and related laws gave legal recognition to the customary rights of upper castes, turning them into owners of land in the modern sense.

The Government of India Act, 1935 gave legal recognition to lists or 'schedules' of castes and tribes marked out for special treatment by the state, origin of the terms Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
So colonialism did not invent caste, but it changed it, making it more rigid and more a matter of official identity.

example.q: How did the act of counting caste in the census change caste itself?
steps: The census asked people to fit into fixed, named caste categories.
In 1901 it also tried to rank castes in a hierarchy.
Castes organised and petitioned for higher rank.
Caste became more rigid and politically important.
example.answer: Official counting froze fluid identities and made caste a matter of state record and competition.

learn.reallife: When state governments today ask for a caste-wise survey, the debate echoes the colonial census: counting categories can shape the identities being counted.

options: Castes petitioned for a higher position

Caste became a purely religious matter

steps: Asks: an effect of ranking castes in the census
Ranking made caste status a matter of official record and competition
Castes therefore petitioned for a higher position

quiz.q: Colonial land revenue settlements affected caste by:
options: Giving all land to the lower castes by law
Removing caste from land ownership completely
Giving upper castes legal property rights over land

Customary rights of upper castes were recognised as legal ownership
So upper castes got legal property rights over land

Answer: Giving upper castes legal property rights over land

options: Abolished untouchability in all provinces
Legally recognised schedules of castes and tribes

It gave legal recognition to lists (schedules) of castes and tribes
These groups were marked for special treatment
Answer: Legally recognised schedules of castes and tribes
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with Article 17 or the census

quiz.q: The terms 'Scheduled Castes' and 'Scheduled Tribes' come from:
options: Lists of groups marked for special state treatment
Times fixed by officials for regular caste meetings

Calendars of temple festivals printed in each region
quiz.explain: The 1935 Act's schedules listed groups for welfare measures.
steps: Asks: the origin of 'Scheduled Castes' and 'Scheduled Tribes'
The 1935 Act listed groups for special state welfare in schedules
So the terms come from these lists
'Schedule' here does not mean a timetable
Answer: Lists of groups marked for special state treatment

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Colonialism made caste more rigid.
Reason (R): Census enumeration fixed caste identities in official categories.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Fixing fluid identities in records made them more rigid.
steps: Check A: colonialism made caste more rigid: true
Check R: census enumeration fixed caste identities in official categories: true
R explains A: fixing fluid identities in records made them rigid
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Misses the link between counting and rigidity

quiz.q: Which statement best sums up colonialism's impact on caste?
options: It created the whole caste system from nothing
It had no effect on caste at all, anywhere
It abolished caste completely by a law of 1901
It did not invent caste but changed it considerably
quiz.explain: Caste predates colonialism, but colonial policies reshaped it.
steps: Asks: the best summary of colonialism's impact on caste
Caste existed before colonial rule, so colonialism did not invent it
But census, land and legal policies reshaped it a great deal
Answer: It did not invent caste but changed it considerably

quiz.q: Why did colonial rulers try to collect information on caste?
options: To abolish caste at once
To promote inter-caste marriage
To understand and govern Indian society
To convert everyone to one religion
quiz.explain: Knowledge of society was seen as necessary for administration.
steps: Asks: why colonial rulers collected caste data
Knowledge of society was seen as necessary to govern it
So to understand and govern Indian society
The British did not aim to abolish caste or promote inter-caste marriage
Answer: To understand and govern Indian society
quiz.mistake: Attributes reformist goals to colonial counting

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Did the British create caste? What did they actually do to it?'
teach.praise: So the British didn't invent caste, but counting, ranking and land laws made it more rigid, and the 1935 Act made schedules. Clever bird, me!
teach.nudge: But which colonial measures affected caste, and how?

revise.summary: Colonial rulers counted and classified caste to govern India, which made caste identities more rigid. Colonialism did not invent caste, but it changed it through the census, land settlements and the 1935 Act's schedules.
focus: The 1901 census under Herbert Risley and its effects
How land revenue settlements gave upper castes legal ownership of land
Government of India Act, 1935 and the origin of 'Scheduled Castes' and 'Scheduled Tribes'
remember: 1901 census (Herbert Risley): tried to record the social hierarchy of castes in each region
Government of India Act, 1935: legal recognition to schedules of castes and tribes marked for special state treatment
Colonialism did not invent caste, but changed it
traps: Counting did not weaken caste; castes petitioned for higher status and identities hardened
'Schedule' means a list, not a timetable
Colonial counting was for governing, not for reform

topics.title: Caste in the present: reform, the state and change

learn.hook: In a metro train, nobody asks your caste before you sit down. But at a wedding, caste often still decides who marries whom. Modern India changed caste in public life far more than in private life.
points: Opposition to caste came from reformers and nationalists: Jyotiba Phule, B.R. Ambedkar and Mahatma Gandhi (in different ways) attacked untouchability and caste discrimination. Abolishing caste was part of the nationalist programme.
The independent state was committed to abolishing caste, yet it also used caste as a basis for reservations to undo historical injustice. This is a contradiction the book highlights.
Industrialisation, urbanisation and education weakened caste rules in public life: factory and office jobs, eating in restaurants and travelling in trains and buses made strict separation hard.
In the cultural and domestic sphere caste has proved resilient, especially endogamy: most marriages still take place within the caste.

example.q: Why does the book call the state's approach to caste 'contradictory'?
steps: The state aimed for a caste-free society.
But to correct past injustice it used caste to define who gets reservations.
So it both sought to abolish caste and gave caste an official role.
example.answer: It wanted to end caste but had to recognise caste to remedy caste-based disadvantage.

learn.reallife: Indian Railways never had caste-wise coaches, and urban offices hire by qualification; yet marriage portals still offer filters by caste. Public change, private continuity.

Ignored caste entirely in every one of its policies

steps: Asks: the contradiction in the state's approach to caste
The state aimed to abolish caste
Yet to remedy caste injustice it had to recognise caste, e.g. for reservations
Answer: Sought to abolish caste but used it for reservations

quiz.q: Which process weakened caste rules in public life?
options: Rising rates of endogamy
Stricter rules about food
Continuing hereditary occupations
Urbanisation and industrial jobs

In factories, offices and transport, people of all castes mix
This made strict separation hard to keep
So urbanisation and industrial jobs
Answer: Urbanisation and industrial jobs

quiz.q: In which sphere has caste proved most resilient?
options: Marriage and the home
Travel by railway
Recruitment in offices
Seating in restaurants
quiz.explain: Endogamy remains strong despite public-sphere change.
steps: Asks: where caste is most resilient
Public-sphere rules have weakened, but endogamy remains strong
So marriage and the home

Answer: Marriage and the home
quiz.mistake: Thinks caste persists mainly in public places

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Most marriages in India still take place within the caste.
Reason (R): Endogamy has weakened as much as caste rules in public life.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Endogamy is the most resilient feature; it has not weakened like public-sphere rules.
steps: Check A: most marriages still take place within caste: true
Check R: endogamy has weakened as much as public-sphere caste rules: false
Endogamy is the most resilient feature of caste
So A true, R false
Answer: A is true, but R is false
quiz.mistake: Assumes change is uniform across spheres

They were used only by upper-caste travellers
They banned all travel by lower-caste people
People of all castes had to travel together

steps: Asks: why railways and buses weakened caste rules
In shared transport, people of all castes had to travel together
So strict separation became impractical

Answer: People of all castes had to travel together

quiz.q: Abolition of caste was part of:
options: The colonial census plan of 1901
The nationalist and reform programme
The traditional jajmani system
The Malthusian theory of population
quiz.explain: Nationalists and reformers made abolition of caste a goal.
steps: Asks: what abolition of caste was part of
Nationalists and social reformers made abolition of caste a goal
So the nationalist and reform programme
The 1901 census ranked castes rather than abolishing them
Answer: The nationalist and reform programme

quiz.q: Which statement about caste today is most accurate?
options: It has disappeared from every sphere of Indian life
It has grown stronger in every single sphere of life
It has weakened in public life but persists in marriage
It now exists only in official census records and lists
quiz.explain: Change has been uneven across public and private spheres.
steps: Asks: the most accurate statement about caste today
Change has been uneven
Caste has weakened in public life but persists in marriage
"It has disappeared from every sphere of Indian life" and "It has grown stronger in every single sphere of life" overstate the change in opposite directions
Answer: It has weakened in public life but persists in marriage

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'Has caste disappeared in modern India? I see people mixing everywhere in the city!'
teach.praise: So caste weakened in trains, offices and restaurants, but endogamy keeps it alive at home. And the state both opposes and uses caste. Tricky!
teach.nudge: But where has caste weakened and where does it still persist?

revise.summary: Reformers and nationalists such as Phule, Ambedkar and Gandhi opposed caste, and the independent state aimed to abolish it while also using it for reservations. Caste has weakened in public life but stays strong in marriage and the home.

How industrialisation, urbanisation, education and transport weakened caste rules in public life
Why caste remains resilient in the cultural and domestic sphere, especially endogamy

topics.title: Caste and politics: dominant castes and visibility

learn.hook: At election time, analysts on TV talk about caste 'arithmetic' in every constituency. Democracy did not end caste; it gave caste a new job.
points: Caste became a basis for political mobilisation: caste associations formed, parties built caste-based support bases or 'vote banks', and castes acted as pressure groups.

M.N. Srinivas's 'dominant castes': castes that are numerically large, own land and hold political power in a region. Many were middle castes that gained from land reforms, e.g. Yadavs (Bihar, UP), Vokkaligas (Karnataka), Reddys and Kammas (Andhra Pradesh), Marathas (Maharashtra), Jats (Punjab, Haryana, western UP) and Patidars (Gujarat).
Sanskritisation, adopting the customs of higher castes, was one route by which castes sought upward mobility.
For urban upper castes caste has become 'invisible': having gained economic and educational capital from caste in the past, they can now claim to be 'caste-less' and rely on merit.
For SC, ST and OBC groups caste has become hyper-visible, because their caste identity is central to claims on reservations and other state protection.

example.q: An urban professional says, 'Caste doesn't matter to me at all.' A villager from a Scheduled Caste says caste shapes everything in his life. How does the book explain both views?
steps: The professional's family may have built education and wealth through past caste privilege.
Now that capital passes on without visible caste help, caste looks 'invisible' to him.
The villager depends on caste-based protections and still faces discrimination, so caste is highly visible.
Both views come from different social positions.

topics.title: Tribe: concept and classification by permanent traits

learn.hook: From the Gonds of central India, numbering in millions, to Andaman island communities of just a few hundred people, 'tribe' covers an astonishing range of communities.
points: 'Tribe' is a modern term, used by colonial and later administrators for communities seen as outside the caste-Hindu fold: no caste, no written-text religion, no state of the usual kind and no sharp class divisions.
Permanent traits used to classify tribes: region, language, physical (racial) characteristics and ecological habitat.
Region: about 85 per cent of the tribal population lives in 'middle India' (from Gujarat and Rajasthan to West Bengal and Odisha); over 11 per cent lives in the North-East.

Language: four families, Indo-Aryan, Dravidian, Austric and Tibeto-Burman. Austric is spoken entirely by tribal people, and over 80 per cent of Tibeto-Burman speakers are tribal. Physical-racial categories once used: Negrito, Australoid, Mongoloid, Dravidian and Aryan.

Size: tribes range from over a million (Gonds, Bhils, Santhals, Oraons, Minas, Bodos, Mundas) to very small groups such as the Andamanese islanders. Tribal people make up about 8 per cent of India's population.

example.q: Which permanent trait is used when tribes are grouped as 'Austric' or 'Tibeto-Burman'?

topics.title: Acquired traits and the debate over 'tribe'

learn.hook: Textbooks once pictured tribes as isolated forest dwellers frozen in time. But Gond kings ruled kingdoms, and tribal chiefs traded and fought alongside states for centuries. The real history is very different.
points: Acquired traits used to classify tribes: (1) mode of livelihood: fishers, food gatherers and hunters, shifting cultivators, peasants, and plantation and industrial workers; (2) extent of incorporation into Hindu society.
Debate: many scholars argue tribes were never isolated or 'primitive'. Many were 'secondary' formations, shaped through long contact with states and civilisations.
Historical evidence: Gond kingdoms of central India (such as Garha Mandla and Chanda); tribal chiefdoms; trading links; tribes serving as soldiers and allies of states.

1940s debate on policy: 'isolationists' or protectionists (associated with Verrier Elwin) wanted tribes protected from traders, moneylenders and missionaries; 'integrationists' (associated with G.S. Ghurye, who saw tribes as 'backward Hindus') wanted them integrated into the mainstream.

example.q: A tribe once practised shifting cultivation; now many members work in a steel plant. Which classification captures this change?
steps: Shifting cultivation and industrial work are modes of livelihood.
Livelihood is an acquired trait, so it can change.
The tribe moves from one livelihood category to another.
example.answer: Classification by mode of livelihood, an acquired trait.

learn.hook: The big dams and steel plants that powered India's growth were often built on tribal land. For those who lost their homes, 'national development' felt very different.
points: After independence, national development, through large dams, mines, industries and forest policies, often came at the cost of tribal communities, who lost land and forests and were displaced.
Tribal identity today is shaped by forced incorporation into the mainstream and by resistance and assertion against it.
Long movements won statehood for Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh in 2000, but problems of displacement and control over resources continue.
In the North-East, special laws (such as the Armed Forces Special Powers Act) limiting civil liberties have been linked to cycles of rebellion and repression.

Reservations have produced an educated tribal middle class that shapes tribal identity and assertion. Two key issues drive tribal movements: control over vital resources (land, forests) and ethnic-cultural identity.

Loss of sacred sites, language and community life threatens ethnic-cultural identity.

example.answer: Control over land and forests, and protection of cultural identity.

learn.hook: Think of your own family: who lives with whom, whose surname you carry, who decides big things. Each answer points to a different way of classifying families.
points: Nuclear family: one couple and their unmarried children. Extended (joint) family: more than one couple, often more than two generations, living together.
It is a myth that India had only joint families: nuclear families have always existed, especially among some groups, and joint families were often an ideal of landed upper castes.

By residence: matrilocal (couple lives with the wife's parents) or patrilocal (with the husband's parents). By inheritance/succession: matrilineal (through the mother) or patrilineal (through the father). By authority: matriarchal (women dominant) or patriarchal (men dominant).
Families change accidentally (war, migration, illness) or through deliberate choices. In many urban families grandparents now move in to help with child care while both parents work.
Marriage is changing too: more love marriages and a higher age at marriage, though inter-caste marriages still face resistance.

example.q: Priya, after marriage, lives with her husband in his parents' house; property passes from father to son; the eldest man makes major decisions. Classify this family.
steps: Living with the husband's parents: patrilocal.
Property from father to son: patrilineal.
Men hold authority: patriarchal.

topics.title: Matriliny, matriarchy and gender: the Khasi example

learn.hook: Among the Khasis of Meghalaya, property passes from mother to daughter. Does that make it a society ruled by women? The answer is a lesson in reading sociological terms carefully.
points: Matrilineal societies in India include the Khasis of Meghalaya and the Nairs of Kerala.
Among the Khasis, property passes from mother to daughter, but control over it rests with the mother's brother (maternal uncle).
This creates role strain for men: they are torn between responsibilities to their natal family (sister's household) and to their wife and children.
Matriliny is not matriarchy: inheritance through women does not mean women hold power. Matriarchy remains a theoretical concept with no clear historical or ethnographic example.
In most Indian families, patriarchal norms and son preference shape decisions on inheritance, education and even survival of girls.

example.q: Explain why a Khasi woman who inherits ancestral property may still not control it.
steps: Khasi descent and inheritance run through women: matriliny.
But managing and controlling property is the job of her brother or maternal uncle.
So ownership by inheritance and authority are separated, and men keep authority.
example.answer: Matriliny gives women inheritance, but authority stays with men, so it is not matriarchy.

learn.reallife: Meghalaya's matrilineal customs often surprise visitors, yet debates there about men's rights and women's role in traditional councils show that inheritance and power are different things.
